title: A weekly act of giving
hookLine: one regular gift, of time or money
tomorrow: full moon tonight, and no temple near the dorm. can Mai keep it?

cards: Mai has a meal card and almost no cash until the program ends. At the Thursday sit, the temple's donation box stood by the door, and she walked past it feeling small. Can a weekly gift be time instead of money?
There's a sound behind the Buddhist answer, if you listen for it: water dripping into a pot.

teach.b: Giving, dana, sits at the start of Buddhist practice. When the Buddha taught newcomers step by step, the suttas say he began with giving, before virtue, before anything harder. And the Dhammapada gives giving its sound.

In Max Müller's translation: "Even by the falling of water-drops a water-pot is filled; the wise man becomes full of good, even if he gather it little by little." Listen to the drops. No single one fills anything.

teach.h: MORE THAN ONE KIND OF GIFT.
teach.b: That's why a weekly gift matters more than its size: it turns generosity from an event into a habit. The suttas also say gifts come in more than one kind.
There's the gift of things, and there's the gift of the teaching itself; temples run on help in the kitchen, a swept floor, a ride for an elder. Ông carries a bag of fruit to the temple every week.
And one short text, the Itivuttaka, has the Buddha say that if people knew, as he did, the fruit of giving and sharing, they wouldn't eat without giving, not even their last bite.
A gift doesn't wait for plenty. It drips.

how: Buddhists practice dana in many forms: food for monks and nuns, gifts to the temple, volunteering in temple kitchens and grounds, and charity; some give on a regular rhythm, such as each week or on moon days.

games.q: what does “a weekly act of giving” mean?
o: a gift given only to family and close friends
one small, regular gift of time or money
a large donation made once at the year's end

games.q: the shape of a gift — tap the pairs.
p: fill the pot, little by little
a bag of fruit to the temple each week

s: in Buddhism, giving only means donating money
the suttas name more than one kind of gift, and help and time count.
the Dhammapada says a water pot is filled even by falling drops
the wise grow full of good the same way, little by little.
the Buddha taught that giving can wait until you have plenty
in the Itivuttaka, if people knew the fruit of giving they wouldn't eat without sharing, even a last bite.

games.q: your aunt plans one large donation at the end of each year. her daughter wants to give a little every week instead. what does today's teaching add?
o: the small weekly gift builds giving into a life, drop by drop, like the pot
only the big yearly gift really counts, because its total is larger
neither counts unless the gift is kept secret from everyone
games.why: the Dhammapada's pot fills by drops. a weekly gift makes giving a rhythm rather than one event; the yearly gift can still be good too.

practice: Hold an empty cup or bowl in both hands, the way an alms bowl is held. Feel its weight with nothing in it, and breathe. With each breath, picture one drop falling in: one small gift, one week at a time.

wordCard.voice: A weekly act of giving: one small gift, of time or money, given on a rhythm, drop by drop.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit: giving, generosity. In the Buddha's step-by-step teaching, the first subject.

carryVoice: The line to keep: every week, a gift, drop by drop until the pot is full. Done for today.

sources.q: Even by the falling of water-drops a water-pot is filled; the wise man becomes full of good, even if he gather it little by little.

sources.ref: Itivuttaka 26 (if beings knew the result of giving and sharing)
the step-by-step talk beginning with giving (e.g. Digha Nikaya 3, Majjhima Nikaya 56); Anguttara Nikaya 2 on the two kinds of gifts, material and of the Dhamma
